title: UNLEAVENED: The Bread of Urgency, the Taste of Freedom, and the God Who Refused to Let Them Stay Bound
paragraphs: UNLEAVENED: The Bread of Urgency, the Taste of Freedom, and the God Who Refused to Let Them Stay Bound
What kind of God interrupts your life so violently that you don’t even have time to let your bread rise?

That’s where this story begins… not in a temple, not in a sermon, not in a quiet devotional moment—but in panic, in midnight, in trembling hands kneading dough that would never have time to become what it once was.
Because when God decides it’s time to free you… He does not wait for your comfort.

In Exodus 12, the command comes with urgency that almost feels uncomfortable to read. The Lord tells Israel to eat quickly, dressed, sandals on, staff in hand, ready to move. And then comes this strange instruction that echoes through generations:

“וַיֹּאכְלוּ אֶת־הַבָּשָׂר… וּמַצּוֹת עַל־מְרֹרִים יֹאכְלֻהוּ”
(Va’yokhlu et-ha’basar… u’matzot al-merorim yokhluhu)
“They shall eat the flesh… and unleavened bread; with bitter herbs they shall eat it.” (Exodus 12:8)
Unleavened bread. מַצּוֹת (matzot). Bread without yeast. Bread without delay.
At first glance, it sounds like a minor dietary detail.
But it is not.
It is a command soaked in urgency, identity, and transformation.

Because yeast—שְׂאֹר (se’or)—was never just about baking. It symbolized process, delay, fermentation… something that slowly spreads, something that changes everything it touches. And in Scripture, it often carries a deeper meaning: influence, corruption, pride, sin quietly expanding beneath the surface.
So God says, remove it.
Not gradually. Not later. Not when it’s convenient.
Now.

“שִׁבְעַת יָמִים מַצּוֹת תֹּאכֵלוּ… אַךְ בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן תַּשְׁבִּיתוּ שְּׂאֹר”
(Shiv’at yamim matzot tokhelu… ach bayom harishon tashbitu se’or)
“Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread… on the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses.” (Exodus 12:15)
Remove it.
Because freedom cannot coexist with what has been silently shaping you in slavery.
And maybe that’s where this starts to feel personal.
Because some of us are still trying to walk into freedom while holding onto what God already told us to remove.
Some habits. Some relationships. Some hidden compromises.
Some “small” things that have been quietly spreading inside us for years.
The Israelites didn’t have time to negotiate with their past. The text makes it painfully clear:

“כִּי גֹרְשׁוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם… וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לְהִתְמַהְמֵהַּ”
(Ki gor’shu miMitzrayim… v’lo yakhlu l’hitmahméha)
“For they were driven out of Egypt… and could not delay.” (Exodus 12:39)
No delay.
No time to let the dough rise.
No time to let their old life “finish.”
Because God was not improving their slavery.
He was ending it.
And that changes everything.
Because unleavened bread is not just about what they ate…
It’s about what they left behind.
It’s about the kind of freedom that doesn’t wait for you to feel ready.
It’s about a God who says, “We are leaving tonight.”
And if you’re honest… that’s uncomfortable.
Because we like gradual change.
We like “I’ll deal with this later.”
We like the idea of freedom… just not the urgency that comes with it.
But the Passover story refuses to let you stay there.
And then… centuries later… something happens that shifts this from history into something deeply personal.
Jesus sits at a table during Passover.
The same unleavened bread.
The same story.
The same memory of deliverance.
And He takes the bread—ἄζυμος (azymos), unleavened—and breaks it.
“This is My body.”
Suddenly, the bread without leaven becomes the body without sin.
Because Jesus is the only one who lived completely unleavened—without corruption, without hidden spread, without compromise.
And He offers Himself.
Not just to remember the Exodus…
But to become it.
Paul later writes:

(katharisate tēn palaian zymēn… hōste ēte neon phyrama)
“Cleanse out the old leaven… that you may be a new lump.” (1 Corinthians 5:7)
Do you see it?
The same call.
Remove it.
Because you are not who you used to be.
Because Christ didn’t just free you from something…
He is forming something new in you.
And this is where it stops being a story about ancient Israel and starts becoming a mirror.
Because the question is no longer, “Why did they eat unleavened bread?”
The question becomes…
What are you still letting rise inside you that God already called you out of?
What Egypt are you still carrying in your heart?
What “leaven” have you learned to tolerate?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because this is not about guilt.
This is about freedom.
Real freedom.
The kind that doesn’t wait for perfect timing.
The kind that interrupts your life and says, “Now.”
And here’s the part many people miss…
Unleavened bread was eaten with bitter herbs.
Because freedom is remembered alongside what it cost.
Because you don’t fully understand grace until you remember the bitterness of where you were.
And that’s why this message matters right now.
Because some of you have forgotten what God brought you out of.
You’ve gotten comfortable.
Numb.
Spiritually passive.
But something in you is waking up again.
And maybe that’s not an accident.
Maybe God is calling you back to a life that moves when He speaks.
A life that doesn’t delay obedience.
A life that removes what doesn’t belong.
A life that understands that holiness is not restriction…
It is freedom.
If this stirred something in you, don’t keep it to yourself.
Because daily, we’re building something deeper here… not surface-level inspiration, but real discipleship.
And if you feel God calling you deeper—into understanding, into growth, into real transformation—there’s more waiting for you.
And for those who choose to stand with this mission, to help spread the Gospel, to reach more souls, to keep truth alive in a world that keeps watering it down…
Not because faith is for sale…
But because mission requires movement.
And if your heart is burning right now, if something inside you is saying, “I want more of God, not less”…
Then don’t stay on the surface.
Because at the end of all this…
Unleavened bread was never just about food.
It was about a God who refuses to let His people stay in chains.
And maybe tonight… He’s still calling people out.
The question is…
Will you leave when He says go?
Some people pray for freedom… but hesitate when it actually arrives.
